claims.claim: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth, at 1,642 metres
claims.definition: Baikal's maximum depth is 1,642 m (modern soundings), making it the deepest lake on Earth and among the deepest lakes ever measured
claims.authoritative_source: Moore et al., 'Lake Baikal: A mirror in time and space' (Geography reviews) and Limnological Institute (SBR RAS) soundings; standard limnological references
claims.notes: narration states the depth figure directly; it is a stable measured value

nuance.note: the 1,642 m maximum depth is the accepted sounding value

claims.claim: Baikal holds roughly one fifth of Earth's unfrozen fresh surface water, more than the North American Great Lakes combined
claims.definition: Baikal's volume is about 23,600 cubic kilometres, commonly cited as roughly 20 percent of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water; that exceeds the combined volume of the five Great Lakes (~22,700 cubic kilometres)
claims.current_record_holder: largest fresh surface-water lake by volume
claims.measured_value: ~23,600 km3; ~20% of unfrozen fresh surface water; spread over North America, depth of about 1 m
claims.authoritative_source: NOAA Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory volume tables; standard limnological references for Baikal volume
claims.notes: narration says 'roughly one fifth' and 'not close'; the 1-m coverage figure is a standard back-of-envelope (23,600 km3 / 24.5M km2)

nuance.note: the ~20% share and the Great-Lakes comparison are standard; the exact percentage cited varies 20-23% with freshwater definitions, hence 'roughly'

claims.claim: Baikal lies in an active continental rift that keeps widening, so the basin keeps deepening
claims.definition: the Baikal Rift Zone is an active divergent boundary where the crust is being pulled apart; sediment records and geodesy indicate continued extension, and the lake basin accumulates sediment and deepens over geologic time
claims.measured_value: qualitative: active rift with continuing extension; narration avoids pinning a spreading rate
claims.authoritative_source: Petit & Deverchere, 'Structure and evolution of the Baikal Rift' (reviews); Logatchev & Florensov classic rift studies; ICDP Baikal Drilling Project
claims.notes: narration deliberately avoids a spreading rate — published estimates vary by method and segment

nuance.note: the rift is active; exact extension rates and deep-basin dynamics vary by study, so narration stays qualitative

claims.claim: at roughly 25 million years Baikal is the world's oldest lake
claims.definition: Baikal is commonly cited as the world's oldest lake, with an age of roughly 25-30 million years based on geological and sediment-core evidence
claims.measured_value: roughly 25-30 million years old; narration says 'some twenty-five million years'
claims.authoritative_source: Baikal Drilling Project sediment records; standard limnological references
claims.notes: narration hedges with 'some twenty-five million years'

nuance.note: Baikal's status as the oldest extant lake is standard; the precise age is a range

claims.claim: most of Baikal's species live nowhere else
claims.definition: a large majority of Baikal species are endemic; commonly cited figures put endemism at roughly 60-80% of species (higher in some groups, e.g., amphipods and fish like the transparent golomyanka)
claims.measured_value: roughly 60-80% endemism depending on taxon; narration says 'most of its species'
claims.authoritative_source: Kozhova & Izmest'eva (eds.), 'Lake Baikal: Evolution and Biodiversity' (1998); standard Baikal biodiversity literature
claims.notes: narration says 'most of its species live nowhere else' without pinning a percentage

nuance.note: high endemism is one of Baikal's defining features; exact shares vary by taxon

claims.claim: the Baikal seal (nerpa) lives and breeds entirely in fresh water, far from any ocean; its route there is debated
claims.definition: the Baikal seal Pusa sibirica is among the few pinnipeds that live and breed entirely in fresh water, roughly a thousand kilometres from the nearest ocean; the colonization route (via the Yenisei/Angara river system from the Arctic, most plausibly during Pleistocene glaciations) remains debated in detail
claims.measured_value: qualitative: exclusively freshwater-living and breeding seal; distance from ocean roughly 1,000 km; narration avoids settling the route
claims.authoritative_source: Pastukhov, 'The Nerpa of Lake Baikal' (biological monographs); standard pinniped literature on Pusa sibirica
claims.notes: narration hedges the origin: 'how its ancestors arrived is still argued about'

nuance.note: the seal's freshwater residency is firmly established; the colonization route and timing are actively discussed, hence hedged
